---
title: "Check your data"
description: "Find out how good your tracking really is — confidence, gaps, and when they happen — before changing anything."
order: 3
---



Tracking data is never perfect. Keypoints get occluded, the tracker guesses,
and a guess looks exactly like a measurement once it's written to file — a pair
of plausible coordinates, indistinguishable from the real thing.

[anicheck](https://animovement.dev/anicheck) exists to tell them apart. Its
functions only *report*: they take an aniframe and give you back a summary,
leaving your data untouched. Cleaning comes next, once you know what you're
cleaning.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(animovement)

movement <- read_sleap(get_sample_data("sleap")) |>
  set_sampling_rate(30)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
#> Downloading sleap data...
```


:::
:::


## How confident was the tracker? {#sec-confidence}

Pose-estimation tools score every point they place. `check_confidence()`
summarises those scores per keypoint:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_confidence(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> ── Check: tracking confidence 
#> Confidence for 6 keypoints (median [min]):
#> • individual1 | centre: 0.93 [0.29]
#> • individual1 | left_ear: 0.96 [0.00]
#> • individual1 | right_ear: 0.89 [0.00]
#> • individual1 | snout: 0.78 [0.00]
#> • individual1 | tail_base: 0.96 [0.00]
#> • individual1 | tail_end: 0.77 [0.00]
```


:::
:::


Already informative: the snout and tail end are tracked far less confidently
than the centre or the ears — which makes sense, they're the parts that
disappear when the mouse turns. Pair the check with `plot()` to see the whole
distribution rather than two numbers:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(check_confidence(movement))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Confidence per keypoint. The spike at zero is the tracker admitting it had no idea.](check-data_files/figure-html/plot-conf-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


This is the plot that picks your threshold. The bulk of each keypoint sits near
1, with a separate clump at zero and a thin tail between — so a cut somewhere
around 0.6 removes the failures without touching the good tracking. Where
exactly to cut is a judgement call about your data, and this plot is how you
make it rather than guess it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Confidence isn't a probability
Scores are whatever the tracker chose to emit. SLEAP's run past 1 in this
recording, and a "0.9" from one tool means nothing about a "0.9" from another.
Read the distribution, don't import a threshold from someone else's paper.
:::

## Where are the gaps? {#sec-gaps}

Missing values are the other half of the story. `check_na_gapsize()` reports how
many there are and, more usefully, how they're distributed between short
dropouts and long absences:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_na_gapsize(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> ── Check: missing-value gap sizes 
#> Tracking x: 9230 missing (8.3%) across 1019 gaps, longest 197 frames.
#> By group (individual and keypoint):
#> • individual1 | centre: 79 gaps, longest 108
#> • individual1 | left_ear: 87 gaps, longest 108
#> • individual1 | right_ear: 86 gaps, longest 108
#> • individual1 | snout: 331 gaps, longest 197
#> • individual1 | tail_base: 109 gaps, longest 108
#> • individual1 | tail_end: 327 gaps, longest 136
```


:::
:::


Eight percent of this recording is missing, but that number hides the shape of
the problem: the snout alone accounts for 331 separate gaps, one of them 197
frames long. Plotting one keypoint at a time shows the shape clearly:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement |>
  dplyr::filter(keypoint == "snout") |>
  check_na_gapsize() |>
  plot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Gap sizes for the snout. Most gaps are a handful of frames; the red bars count gaps, the blue bars count the missing values they add up to.](check-data_files/figure-html/plot-gaps-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


That distinction matters for the next step. A one-frame gap is worth
interpolating across — the mouse can't have gone far. A 197-frame gap is nearly
seven seconds, and anything you draw across it is invention.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Plotting several groups at once
These check plots put each group in its own panel, so with six keypoints you'll
want a taller figure — `fig-height: 10` or so — before they become readable.
One keypoint at a time is usually easier to read anyway.
:::

## When do they happen? {#sec-timing}

Gaps clustered in one stretch mean something different from gaps sprinkled
evenly — a lighting change, say, versus a keypoint the model was never good at.
`check_na_timing()` splits the recording into intervals and shows what fraction
of each is missing:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
check_na_timing(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> ── Check: timing of missing values 
#> Tracking x across 110910 frames - 9230 missing (8.3%) in 1019 gaps.
#> By group (individual and keypoint):
#> • individual1 | centre: 2.7% missing in 79 gaps (longest 108)
#> • individual1 | left_ear: 2.8% missing in 87 gaps (longest 108)
#> • individual1 | right_ear: 2.9% missing in 86 gaps (longest 108)
#> • individual1 | snout: 24.3% missing in 331 gaps (longest 197)
#> • individual1 | tail_base: 3.8% missing in 109 gaps (longest 108)
#> • individual1 | tail_end: 13.5% missing in 327 gaps (longest 136)
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement |>
  dplyr::filter(keypoint == "snout") |>
  check_na_timing() |>
  plot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![When the snout goes missing. Nearly half of some early intervals, barely any of others.](check-data_files/figure-html/plot-timing-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Here it's spread across the whole recording, with a couple of bad patches near
the start and around eight minutes in — the mouse in the closed arms, out of
sight of the camera. Nothing to fix in the setup; something to be careful about
when interpreting behaviour from those stretches.

## What we learned {#sec-summary}

Three checks, three decisions for the [next guide](process-data.qmd):

- The maze occupies roughly x ∈ [300, 1010], y ∈ [0, 690]; the few points
  outside it are impossible, so they can go.
- Confidence separates cleanly around **0.6**, so that's where we'll mask.
- Most gaps are a few frames long and safe to interpolate; a handful run to
  nearly 200 frames and are not.
- The missing data is spread through the recording rather than concentrated in
  one broken stretch, so there's no reason to discard part of it.

Next: [process the trajectories](process-data.qmd).
